title: Legal Research
summary: Learn to research the law effectively: sources and hierarchy of law, finding current legislation, reading cases and precedent, a step-by-step research strategy, writing legal analysis with IRAC, and ethics, AI tools and access to justice.
audience: Law students, paralegals, researchers, journalists and officials who need to find and use the law

body.p: Legal research means finding, reading and applying the law that governs a question. It begins with knowing where law comes from. In most African countries, the sources form a hierarchy.

list: The constitution: the supreme law.
Legislation: acts of parliament, and subsidiary or delegated legislation such as regulations, rules and by-laws made under those acts.
Case law: decisions of the courts, which interpret legislation and develop the law. Under the doctrine of precedent, lower courts follow the decisions of higher courts.
Common law or civil law traditions inherited from colonial systems: English common law in many countries, Roman-Dutch law in Southern Africa, and French or Portuguese civil law in others.
Customary law: the living law of communities, recognised by many constitutions where consistent with rights.
Religious law in some areas, such as Islamic law in personal matters in some countries.
International law: treaties and customary international law, which may apply directly or after being domesticated.

body.p: Primary sources are the law itself: constitutions, statutes and judgments. Secondary sources explain the law: textbooks, journal articles, commentaries and law reform reports. Secondary sources are excellent starting points but must be checked against primary sources.

body.tip: Always identify which legal system applies before researching; the same question may be answered differently in common-law and civil-law countries.

body.p: Legislation is published in the government gazette and collected in official law reports and databases.

list: Free online sources include national Legal Information Institutes, such as SAFLII (South Africa), Kenya Law, ULII (Uganda) and ZambiaLII, and the regional AfricanLII network.
Parliament websites publish bills and acts.
Government gazettes publish regulations, notices and commencement dates.

body.h: Checking that the law is current

steps: Check whether it is in force, and the commencement date of each section.
Find all amendments; use a consolidated (updated) version where available.
Check regulations made under the act.
Check whether courts have interpreted or struck down any sections.

body.p: An act can be amended many times over the years; relying on an old printed copy is a common and serious mistake.

body.tip: Note the date you checked each source; the law may change after you finish your research.

body.p: Judgments explain how courts apply the law to facts. A case citation tells you how to find it, typically with the parties' names, year, court or law report, and page or number.

list: Facts: what happened.
Issues: the legal questions the court had to decide.
Arguments of the parties.
Reasoning: the court's analysis of the law.
Order: what the court decided, for example dismissing or upholding an appeal.

body.p: The ratio decidendi is the legal principle necessary for the decision; it is binding on lower courts. Obiter dicta are other remarks made in passing; they can be persuasive but are not binding. Courts may also distinguish a precedent by showing that the facts of a new case are materially different.

Courts in one African country often cite decisions from others and from international bodies. For example, constitutional judgments from South Africa and Kenya are frequently cited across the continent.

body.tip: Write a short case note for every important case: facts, issue, decision, reasoning and why it matters to your question.

steps: Understand the facts and identify the legal issues. Break a broad problem into specific questions.
Identify key words and legal concepts, including synonyms (for example, "dismissal", "termination" and "retrenchment").
Start with a secondary source to get an overview and leads to primary sources.
Find and read the relevant legislation.
Find cases interpreting it, starting with the highest courts and the most recent decisions.
Check that each authority is still good law: not overruled, amended or repealed.
Record your sources and search steps as you go.
Stop when new searches keep returning the same authorities.

body.p: Customary law may be found in court decisions, restatements, ethnographic studies and evidence from community members and traditional leaders. Researchers must be careful to reflect the living law, which changes, and to respect constitutional rights.

body.tip: Search engines are a starting point, not an authority; always find the official text.

body.p: IRAC is a simple structure for legal answers and memos.

list: Issue: state the legal question precisely.
Rule: set out the relevant law, with citations to legislation and cases.
Application: apply the rule to the facts, considering arguments on both sides.
Conclusion: give a clear answer, noting any uncertainty.

body.p: A research memo typically includes the question presented, a brief answer, the facts, the discussion and a conclusion with recommendations. Write in plain language, use headings, and put the answer near the start so a busy reader can find it.

Cite every source accurately so readers can check it. Follow the citation style required by your institution or court. Copying others' words or ideas without acknowledgment is plagiarism, a serious academic and professional offence.

body.tip: Distinguish clearly between what the law is and what you argue it should be.

lessons.title: Ethics, AI tools and access to justice

body.p: Legal researchers have duties to be accurate, honest and diligent. Lawyers must not mislead the court, including by failing to disclose binding authority against their client's position.

list: AI tools can summarise documents and suggest search terms, but they can invent cases and quotations that do not exist. Courts in several countries have criticised lawyers who submitted fake AI-generated citations.
Always verify every case, statute and quotation in an official source before relying on it.
Protect client confidentiality: do not paste confidential information into tools that may store or share it.

body.p: Free legal information portals, plain-language guides, paralegal networks and university law clinics help people who cannot afford lawyers understand their rights. Legal researchers can contribute by writing clear summaries of important laws and judgments.

body.tip: If you cannot find the original source of a legal claim, do not use it.
